summary: Jon Postel suggests using eight-character standard host names and gives a list pairing network site numbers with standard and alternate names. It is part of a debate on how to name hosts. It was replaced by RFC 236.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 229 suggests eight-character names for ARPA Network hosts and lists names alongside site numbers. Some entries also have alternate names.

questions: what names did rfc 229 suggest for arpanet hosts
subtitle: A proposal for eight-character names for hosts on the ARPA Network.

tldr.problem: Several sets of host names were in use, and a common set was needed for NCPs, Telnets, and hardcopy identification.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC suggests eight-character names and lists formal and alternate names alongside network site numbers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 229 was an informational host-name proposal and was obsoleted by RFC 236.

today: RFC 229 was a host-name proposal and has been obsoleted by RFC 236.

sections.title: A Shared Set of Host Names
sections.content:
The memo says a standard set of names was needed for NCPs and Telnets to identify hosts, and for identifying a person's affiliation in hardcopy. Several sets of names were already in use.

Jon Postel suggests using names of 8 characters and provides a table of host names and network addresses. The memo is a proposal, not a protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Different names were being used for network hosts. This proposal offers one list of names that NCPs and Telnets could recognize.

sections.title: Names and Network Addresses
sections.content:
The table pairs site numbers with standard names and, in some cases, alternate names. For example, site 1 is listed as UCLA-NMC with alternate name SEX; site 65 is UCLA-CCN with alternate name CCN; and site 2 is SRI-ARC with alternate name NIC.

The list includes entries for research and government sites, as well as Terminal IMPs. Several entries have no alternate name shown.
sections.plainLanguage: Look up a site number to find its proposed host name. A few sites also have a shorter alternate name listed.

sections.title: Status of the Proposal
sections.content:
The RFC is a suggested naming list. Its title section identifies RFC 226 as related, and it contains no implementation rules for how a host must use the names.

The unit metadata records RFC 236 as the document that later obsoleted RFC 229.
sections.plainLanguage: This was a naming proposal rather than a required naming standard. A later RFC replaced it.

references.text: Kalin, M. D., "Standardization of Host Mnemonics", RFC 226, September 1971.
